paragraphs: The paper models how people recall words after studying a list. Its central idea is that remembering depends on an internal context that changes gradually as words are encountered. Drawing on psychological research and topic models of documents, it represents both word meanings and this context as distributions over topics.

The model assumes that studying a word incorporates some of its meaning into the evolving context. During recall, that context is reinstated and serves as a retrieval cue. This makes recall a dynamic process: the hidden context helps explain which studied words become available for retrieval, while Bayesian inference represents uncertainty about the underlying cognitive process.

The authors develop a particle filter to approximate the model’s posterior distribution and evaluate predictions of recalled words using experimental data. A hierarchical formulation also captures differences between participants. The contribution is a probabilistic account connecting semantic representations, changing context, and individual variation within one model of recall.
neurips-2009-a-bayesian-analysis-of-dyna.tldr: A Bayesian model explains free recall through word meanings interacting with a gradually changing internal context.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to train conditional random fields using both labeled and unlabeled examples. Its objective combines conditional likelihood on labeled data with mutual information on unlabeled data. This gives the unlabeled examples a role in training through an information-based criterion, alongside the direct supervision supplied by known labels.

The authors connect this objective to rate distortion theory, providing an information-theoretic framework for the learning problem. They distinguish it from approaches that minimize conditional entropy. For structured predictions, the computational challenge is that summing over possible label configurations can involve a combinatorial number of terms. The paper analyzes tractability and develops a convergent variational training algorithm to address that difficulty.

Experiments cover both multiclass classification and sequence labeling. In those experiments, the proposed approach outperforms standard l2 regularization and minimum conditional entropy regularization. These findings support the usefulness of the information-based objective across the two evaluated prediction settings, while the variational algorithm makes the structured training problem computationally manageable.
neurips-2009-a-rate-distortion-approach-.tldr: An information-theoretic training objective helps conditional random fields use unlabeled data and improves results on classification and sequence labeling experiments.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization problems that arise when fitting a model involves a nonsmooth loss or regularizer. Examples include hinge loss and l1 regularization. Ordinary gradient-based methods are attractive because they are simple and scalable, but their convergence can be slow in these settings. The authors seek faster progress while retaining those practical advantages.

Their algorithm, SAGE, introduces acceleration into stochastic gradient optimization. The paper establishes fast convergence rates for both convex and strongly convex objectives. These are two explicitly identified classes of optimization problems for which the method’s convergence behavior is studied. The approach is designed to preserve the computational simplicity and scalability that make gradient methods useful.

Experimental comparisons find SAGE faster than FOLOS, SMIDAS, and SCD, the recent gradient or subgradient methods examined in the paper. The authors also extend the approach to online learning. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support acceleration as a way to improve optimization speed without abandoning a relatively simple learning procedure.
neurips-2009-accelerated-gradient-method.tldr: SAGE accelerates stochastic gradient optimization while preserving simplicity and scalability, with an extension to online learning.

paragraphs: Image retrieval requires similarity measures that capture meaningful relationships as well as visual resemblance. The paper introduces OASIS, a method for learning pairwise similarity at large scale. It addresses the computational difficulty of existing approaches, particularly when high-dimensional data and constraints requiring a mathematical metric make learning expensive.

OASIS learns a bilinear similarity model online using sparse representations, a large-margin criterion, and an efficient hinge-loss objective. Its scaling is linear in the number of objects and nonzero features. This combination ties the computation to the populated features in the data and supports learning across a wide range of collection sizes.

On a benchmark containing thousands of images, OASIS is more precise than the compared state-of-the-art methods and faster by orders of magnitude. Training on two million web images takes three days on one CPU. The authors also transform learned nonmetric similarities into metric similarities, obtaining higher precision than learning metrics directly. This suggests a route to metric learning on substantially larger datasets.
neurips-2009-an-online-algorithm-for-lar.tldr: OASIS learns image similarities efficiently at large scale through online updates to a sparse bilinear model.

paragraphs: The paper develops Bayesian methods for extracting maps of visual-cortex organization from functional imaging measurements. Its main application is estimating orientation preference maps from intrinsic signal imaging. The aim is to infer the underlying spatial pattern while also representing uncertainty about the features of that pattern.

The authors model the map with a bivariate Gaussian process. Its prior covariance reflects known properties of orientation maps, while the noise covariance is adjusted to the data. Within this probabilistic model, the posterior mean provides an optimally smoothed map estimate. The same model supports interpolation when measurements are sparse, connecting observed locations through the assumed spatial structure.

Sampling from the posterior provides error bars for properties such as preferred orientations and the locations or counts of pinwheels. The model is demonstrated on simulated data and recordings from ferret visual cortex. Its value extends beyond producing a single map: it makes uncertainty explicit, gives parameters an interpretable probabilistic basis, and provides groundwork for decoding studies.
neurips-2009-bayesian-estimation-of-orie.tldr: A Gaussian-process model estimates visual-cortex orientation maps and quantifies uncertainty in their spatial features.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a multivariate Laplace prior for Bayesian source localization. The prior encourages sparse explanations while allowing constraints both within individual sources and between sources. This combination matters when a localization model needs to favor limited activity while still representing relationships among possible sources.

The distribution is expressed as a scale mixture that couples source variances rather than their means. In this representation, the connections act through the sources’ variability. The authors show that properties of the scale mixture make expectation propagation efficient for approximating posterior marginals. The remaining computational bottleneck is obtaining diagonal entries of the inverse of a sparse matrix.

The approach is illustrated with a mismatch negativity paradigm using MEG measurements and structural MRI. In that application, spatial coupling produces sources active over larger cortical areas than an uncoupled prior does. The example shows how the prior’s dependency structure changes the spatial extent of inferred activity, alongside the paper’s contribution of an efficient approximate inference method.
neurips-2009-bayesian-source-localizatio.tldr: A multivariate Laplace prior combines sparse Bayesian source localization with dependencies that can produce more spatially extended activity.

paragraphs: The paper adapts boosting to problems where the spatial arrangement of predictive information matters. It adds a spatial regularization kernel to the usual loss formulation, so the learning objective incorporates spatial relationships. This is particularly useful when a trained classifier is also used to locate informative regions in the data.

From that objective, the authors derive an efficient boosting algorithm with additional weights or priors on the base classifiers. They prove a grouping effect: the algorithm encourages selection of spatially local base classifiers that carry discriminative information. The result concerns an encouragement toward joint selection, allowing nearby informative components to appear together in the learned classifier.

The stated primary application is recovering the spatial pattern of discriminative information, with voxel selection in fMRI as an example. In such a setting, the arrangement of selected components is itself part of what the researcher wants to understand. The authors demonstrate performance on several datasets, supporting the use of spatial structure within the boosting framework.
neurips-2009-boosting-with-spatial-regul.tldr: Spatially regularized boosting encourages nearby informative base classifiers to be selected together, helping reveal discriminative spatial patterns.

paragraphs: Conditional Neural Fields address sequence-labeling problems in which the relationship between input features and output labels is nonlinear. The paper starts from conditional random fields with linear potential functions and argues that those functions cannot accurately represent some complex relationships found in applications such as protein structure prediction and handwriting recognition.

The proposed model inserts one or more intermediate layers between inputs and outputs. These layers contain parameterized hidden gates that act as neural-network nodes or local feature extractors. Their purpose is to capture nonlinear relationships while retaining a conditional probabilistic graphical model for sequence labeling. The authors also introduce evidence-based hyperparameter optimization to better control model complexity.

Experiments on two established benchmarks indicate significant improvements over several popular methods. The model ranks best among roughly ten methods examined for protein secondary structure prediction and among a few of the best for handwriting recognition. These results support the practical value of learning nonlinear features within the sequence model on the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2009-conditional-neural-fields-6.tldr: Conditional Neural Fields add hidden nonlinear feature extractors to sequence models and achieve strong results on protein and handwriting benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper seeks to explain how motor-cortex neurons adapt during neuroprosthetic control. Earlier monkey experiments found selective changes when a device misinterpreted some neurons’ preferred movement directions. The affected neurons changed their tuning more than other neurons, suggesting that the system could compensate for errors in how activity was translated into control.

The authors show that a simple learning rule can account for these observations. Neuronal noise supplies exploratory variation, and a global reward signal modulates Hebbian updates to connection weights. Unlike many earlier reward-modulated Hebbian rules, this rule requires no additional information specifying which activity is signal and which is noise.

In the model system, the rule can optimize performance within biologically realistic periods and under high noise levels. When noise is fitted to experimental data, the resulting learning resembles the changes observed in monkeys. The findings support this mechanism as a possible explanation for selective neural adaptation, linking local weight changes and global reward to the observed reorganization.
neurips-2009-functional-network-reorgani.tldr: A reward-modulated Hebbian rule using neuronal noise can reproduce selective adaptation observed during neuroprosthetic control.

paragraphs: The paper proposes measuring human learning capacity with Rademacher complexity, a concept from computational learning theory. It measures how well a learner can fit random data. That ability matters because fitting a training sample can reflect both learning useful structure and accommodating noise, with different implications for performance beyond that sample.

The authors review how Rademacher complexity connects observed training error to a bound on true error. They then introduce an experimental procedure that asks people to learn noise, making the complexity measurable for human learners. This brings a theoretical measure of flexibility into an experimental setting where its dependence on the task and sample size can be examined.

The studies find that human Rademacher complexity can be measured and varies with domain and training-set size in intuitive ways. Human learning in these studies respects the generalization bounds, which can help predict overfitting risk. The paper also discusses potential cognitive-science applications, suggesting a quantitative connection between learning capacity and generalization.
neurips-2009-human-rademacher-complexity.tldr: Experiments measuring how people learn random data connect human learning capacity to theoretical bounds on generalization and overfitting.

paragraphs: The Indian buffet process provides a probability distribution over binary matrices for Bayesian models of features. Such matrices represent whether particular features occur in particular observations. The paper develops a three-parameter extension with power-law behavior, broadening the kinds of feature-occurrence patterns that this modeling framework can describe.

The construction begins with the beta process underlying the ordinary Indian buffet process. The authors generalize it into a stable-beta process and derive the corresponding feature distribution. This gives the extension a probabilistic foundation. They also identify relationships with the Pitman–Yor process, another Bayesian nonparametric process associated with power-law behavior.

The authors apply the resulting model to word occurrences in documents and report improved performance over the ordinary Indian buffet process. This application shows the practical relevance of allowing a different pattern of feature frequencies. The contribution combines a new stochastic-process construction with evidence that its power-law behavior can be useful for modeling document data.
neurips-2009-indian-buffet-processes-wit.tldr: A three-parameter Indian buffet process introduces power-law feature behavior and improves modeling of word occurrences over the ordinary process.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when examples have several possible views, but some views are missing. It assumes that view-generating functions can approximately supply the missing information. Multilingual document classification provides the motivating example: a document may exist in only some languages, while machine translation can generate versions in others.

The authors derive a generalization-error bound for classifiers trained with these artificially created views. The bound reveals a trade-off involving the amount of training data, the number of views, and the quality of the functions that generate them. Consequently, additional views are beneficial in particular circumstances identified by the analysis, rather than being automatically useful whenever they can be created.

Experiments on a subset of Reuters RCV1/RCV2 support this trade-off: translated views may significantly improve classification in the identified cases. The framework also extends naturally to semi-supervised learning with unlabeled multiview data. The result gives a theoretical basis for judging when approximate additional representations can strengthen a classifier.
neurips-2009-learning-from-multiple-part.tldr: A generalization bound identifies when approximately generated views, such as machine translations, can improve classification.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a kernel formed from a polynomial combination of base kernels. Its analysis focuses on regression using kernel ridge regression. Learning the combination makes the kernel itself part of the fitting problem, allowing the method to determine how the supplied base kernels should contribute through a nonlinear combination.

The authors analyze the resulting kernel-learning optimization problem and show that its minimax formulation can be reduced to a simpler minimization. They also prove that a global solution always lies on the boundary of this problem’s feasible region. These results characterize the optimization being solved and provide a foundation for the proposed computational method.

The algorithm uses projection-based gradient descent. Empirically, it converges in few iterations, and extensive experiments on several public datasets demonstrate the technique’s effectiveness. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical simplification of polynomial kernel learning with a practical optimization procedure, with rapid convergence reported as an experimental observation.
neurips-2009-learning-non-linear-combina.tldr: The paper simplifies polynomial kernel learning for ridge regression and develops a projected-gradient algorithm with encouraging empirical performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the choice between gathering information and using existing knowledge to obtain reward. This balance becomes harder when an agent cannot fully observe its environment’s state. The authors propose a dual-policy method that jointly learns the agent’s behavior and how to balance exploration with exploitation in these partially observable environments.

The framework accommodates two forms of information gathering. An agent can take exploratory actions that reveal more about its environment, or it can ask an oracle for optimal actions while paying an associated cost. Which form of exploration is used depends on the problem. Bringing both into one method connects ordinary exploration with active learning.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees concerning the optimality of the exploration–exploitation balance and demonstrates effectiveness on benchmark problems. Its contribution is to make the balancing decision part of what the agent learns. This explicitly incorporates the value of acquiring information, including situations where useful guidance is available but costly.
neurips-2009-learning-to-explore-and-exp.tldr: A dual-policy method learns behavior and the exploration–exploitation balance, including exploration through costly oracle queries.

paragraphs: The paper asks when local updates can efficiently find a nearly optimal maximum a posteriori assignment in a pairwise Markov random field. The proposed randomized algorithm starts from any assignment. Each iteration chooses a random node, selects an appropriately randomized neighborhood around it, and optimizes the assignment within that neighborhood.

The main guarantee applies to graphs with polynomial growth, described as having geometry. For any such n-node pairwise model, the algorithm finds a near-optimal assignment within 2n ln n iterations on average and with high probability. The approximation error depends on the graph’s geometric growth rate and the average radius of the selected neighborhoods.

This dependence creates a trade-off between local computational effort and approximation quality. Neighborhood size affects both the work required by an update and the resulting error guarantee, so the iteration count does not by itself describe all computation. Extensive simulations find very good approximate solutions across several kinds of models with the required geometry.
neurips-2009-local-rules-for-global-map-.tldr: Randomized neighborhood optimization has near-optimal MAP guarantees for pairwise graphical models whose graphs have polynomial growth.

paragraphs: The paper develops a graphical model to help developers locate defects in software. Its evidence comes from execution traces: records of the code positions visited during program runs. Training uses passing tests, allowing the model to learn a probability distribution over transition patterns associated with those successful executions.

When a test fails, the model examines its execution trace and identifies the least likely transition pattern under the learned distribution. That pattern guides attention toward code that may contain a defect. The method therefore turns differences between passing and failing executions into a probabilistic clue about where a developer should investigate.

The authors design the Bernoulli graph model so that Bayesian inference has a closed-form solution. This supplies an explicit computational procedure for analyzing the traces and identifying the unusual pattern. They evaluate the approach using data from AspectJ and Rhino. The contribution is a debugging aid that uses learned execution behavior to prioritize suspicious code locations for further inspection.
neurips-2009-localizing-bugs-in-program-.tldr: A graphical model trained on passing executions flags unlikely transitions in failing runs to guide bug localization.

paragraphs: The paper proposes measuring model complexity as a property in its own right. Many existing measures combine complexity with how well a model describes data. The authors instead focus on the breadth of outcomes a model can accommodate, treating that breadth as the key expression of its flexibility.

Their measure, Prior Predictive Complexity, incorporates the number of parameters, the model’s functional form, parameter ranges, and the parameter prior. Including the prior matters because it is part of the probabilistic model and affects its complexity. Counting parameters alone therefore does not capture all the ingredients that this measure is designed to consider.

PPC measures how wide the model’s range of outcomes is through its prior predictive behavior. The authors describe the measure as intuitive and easy to compute. Its conceptual contribution is a unified way to account for several sources of model flexibility while keeping the complexity question distinct from descriptive adequacy on a particular dataset.
neurips-2009-measuring-model-complexity-.tldr: Prior Predictive Complexity measures model flexibility through the breadth of possible outcomes, accounting for parameters, functional form, ranges, and priors.

paragraphs: The paper addresses updating a trained support vector machine when several training examples are added or removed. Existing incremental and decremental methods efficiently handle a single example. Applying those updates repeatedly becomes time-consuming when the change involves many examples, creating a bottleneck for models whose training data must be refreshed frequently.

The proposed algorithm handles multiple additions or removals simultaneously. It extends the parametric-programming idea underlying the single-example method into multi-parametric programming. This changes the optimization machinery so that a group of training-set changes can be treated together, making multiple-example updates computationally more efficient.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets indicate that the method can substantially reduce the cost of these updates. The authors highlight online SVM learning as a particularly useful setting: old examples must be removed while new examples are incorporated within a short time. The contribution concerns making those model-maintenance operations faster when data changes arrive in groups.
neurips-2009-multiple-incremental-decrem.tldr: A multi-parametric SVM update algorithm reduces computation when multiple training examples are added or removed together.

paragraphs: The paper models texture through both its recurring elements and their spatial arrangement. A two-dimensional hidden Markov model represents an image, with hidden states assigning texton clusters and a transition matrix describing compatibility between adjacent textons. This connects the vocabulary of texture elements to how those elements fit together across the image.

The model is coupled to a hierarchical Dirichlet process. This allows the number of textons and the complexity of their transition relationships to grow as the input texture becomes more irregular. At the same time, the Dirichlet-process prior penalizes complexity and favors regular textures. The framework learns the vocabulary and spatial layout jointly and automatically.

The resulting representation is compact and supports fast texture synthesis with rendering quality comparable to the state-of-the-art image-based rendering methods considered. The authors also demonstrate applications to image segmentation and synthesis. The approach’s central value is its ability to adapt representational complexity while learning local texture components and their spatial organization together.
neurips-2009-nonparametric-bayesian-text.tldr: A Bayesian texture model jointly learns texture elements and spatial relationships while adapting its complexity to texture irregularity.

paragraphs: The paper accelerates inference for latent Dirichlet allocation by running two established methods on graphics processors: collapsed Gibbs sampling and collapsed variational Bayes. Its focus is making effective use of parallel hardware while managing the memory constraints that arise when training models on large datasets.

The authors introduce a data-partitioning scheme that reduces memory requirements, balances computation across multiprocessors, and helps avoid conflicting memory accesses. They also use streaming to accommodate extremely large datasets. These choices address how data and work are distributed, enabling the inference procedures to use the available parallel resources efficiently.

Experiments produce models with the same predictive power as sequential training, with speedups of 26 times for Gibbs sampling and 196 times for variational Bayes on a GPU with 30 multiprocessors. Speedup scales almost linearly with the available multiprocessor count in the reported results. The authors also identify the partitioning and streaming techniques as readily transferable to many other machine-learning models.
neurips-2009-parallel-inference-for-late.tldr: GPU partitioning and streaming substantially accelerate two LDA inference methods while preserving predictive power in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper introduces approximate bilinear programming for value-function approximation, motivated by the lack of useful advance error guarantees in many existing methods. Its formulation provides strong a priori guarantees and provably finds an approximate value function minimizing the Bellman residual, a measure of inconsistency with the value-function equations.

The guarantee comes with a computational challenge: solving a bilinear program globally is NP-hard. The authors explain that this difficulty reflects the underlying objective, since Bellman-residual minimization is itself NP-hard. They therefore employ and analyze a common approximate algorithm for bilinear programs, distinguishing practical computation from the globally optimal formulation.

Their analysis shows that this algorithm provides a convergent generalization of approximate policy iteration. On a simple benchmark, the proposed approach consistently minimizes the Bellman residual. The paper thus links a principled approximation objective and theoretical guarantees to an implementable iterative method, while explicitly recognizing the computational hardness of obtaining the global optimum.
neurips-2009-robust-value-function-appro.tldr: A bilinear formulation gives guarantees for Bellman-residual minimization and motivates a convergent approximation algorithm despite NP-hard global optimization.

paragraphs: The paper addresses two problems with graph-Laplacian approaches to semi-supervised regression: a tendency toward constant solutions and weak extrapolation. It proposes replacing that regularization with second-order Hessian energy. The change alters which kinds of functions the method prefers when learning from labeled examples together with the structure of the remaining data.

In particular, when the data lie on or near a low-dimensional submanifold, Hessian energy favors functions that vary linearly with the data’s natural parameters. This preference allows meaningful variation along the underlying data structure. The authors present it as a way to overcome both the constant-solution bias and the extrapolation problem.

That property also suits semi-supervised dimensionality reduction, where a few labeled points help identify the data’s natural parameters. Experimental results suggest advantages over Laplacian-regularized semi-supervised regression and standard supervised methods. They also support the method’s suitability for dimensionality reduction, connecting the chosen smoothness penalty to the desired behavior of the learned representation.
neurips-2009-semi-supervised-regression-.tldr: Hessian-energy regularization addresses constant-solution bias and weak extrapolation, with promising results for semi-supervised regression and dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: The paper examines how possible occlusion influences perceived depth. Perceptual cues are often described as noisy measurements combined according to their precision. Here, a background cue also provides structural information: the possibility that something is hidden imposes a soft constraint on the target’s location, shifting its perceived position forward.

The authors develop an ideal-observer model that incorporates this structural or depth-ordering information and fit it to human performance in a stereo-matching task. They then change the task’s uncertainty to test whether people use ordinal cues probabilistically. This tests the model through predicted behavioral changes as the reliability of the available information changes.

The model accurately predicts shifts in participants’ behavior. The findings indicate that depth perception involves probabilistic estimates of which surfaces are in front of others, together with estimates of scene structure. The contribution is evidence that perceived depth depends on inferred relationships among scene elements as well as the precision of individual cues.
neurips-2009-structural-inference-affect.tldr: An ideal-observer model predicts how possible occlusion and uncertainty shift human depth judgments.

paragraphs: Partially observable Markov decision processes support planning when actions can either gather information or obtain reward. Specifying such a model can be difficult because both its structure and its many parameters may be unclear. The paper targets the structural part of this problem, extending beyond learning parameters for a model whose state-space size is already known.

The proposed infinite POMDP does not require that size in advance. It assumes that the number of visited states grows as the agent explores, and it explicitly represents only states that have been visited. This allows the represented state space to expand with experience, making the amount of modeled structure responsive to exploration.

The authors demonstrate the model’s utility on several standard problems. The main contribution is a formulation that accommodates uncertainty about how many states the environment requires. It addresses a practical obstacle to constructing partially observable planning models when domain knowledge alone cannot supply the full state-space structure.
neurips-2009-the-infinite-partially-obse.tldr: The infinite POMDP allows the represented state space to grow during exploration without requiring its size in advance.

paragraphs: The paper combines two ways of modeling neural spike trains: history-dependent conditional firing rates and non-Poisson renewal processes. Its conditional renewal model captures effects in both real time and rescaled time. The authors show how to fit it by maximum likelihood using the time-rescaling theorem.

The analysis identifies an important restriction on optimization. For modulated renewal models, the log-likelihood is concave in the linear-filter parameters only when the renewal density satisfies certain restrictive conditions. These exclude several popular choices, including gamma densities with shape parameter different from one. The result suggests that estimating real-time history effects is easier than estimating non-Poisson renewal properties.

The paper also examines model assessment. Tests based on time rescaling quantify relative-time effects, but do not reliably measure accuracy in predicting spikes or modeling stimulus–response relationships. This distinction affects how a successful goodness-of-fit result should be interpreted. Applications to real and simulated neural data illustrate the combined model and its use.
neurips-2009-time-rescaling-methods-for-.tldr: A conditional renewal model combines spike-history effects with non-Poisson timing and exposes limits of optimization and time-rescaling assessments.
